# The Cormorant Tide

<!-- Generated by story build. -->

# Chapter 1: The Body at St Osyth's Eye

The sea gave Adrian Rusk back at dawn.

It did so without ceremony, withdrawing from the causeway stone by stone until the first constable on scene could see the black shape lying between the third and fourth marker posts. Above him the cormorants stood on the ruined roof of St Osyth's Eye, wings opened like undertakers' coats, drying themselves in the cold light.

Detective Inspector Rowan Bell arrived twenty minutes later with sand already in her shoes and the taste of bad coffee at the back of her throat. She had driven from Lewes through lanes silvered with rain, past fields where sheep stood stunned and white against the morning. Pelham Hard appeared at the last bend, harbour masts pricking the sky, gulls ragging one another over the fish quay, the chalk headland turning pink as if the day meant to be pretty in spite of itself.

She had not worked a death here before. She had worked burglaries, missing teenagers, assaults outside pubs, and one deeply stupid dispute about lobster pots that had produced a knife but no lasting injury. A body on the causeway was different. The town would feel it underfoot.

DS Kit Shaw was waiting by the cordon in a navy waterproof, hair flattened to his skull.

"Local historian," he said. "Dr Adrian Rusk. Sixty-four. Found by a dog walker at six ten, once the tide started to clear the stones."

"Dog walker crossed the cordon?"

"Dog crossed the cordon. Owner followed. Dog disappointed by our response."

Rowan looked past him. The causeway ran from the shingle beach to the island in a shallow curve, a spine of old stone usually hidden by water. Warning boards stood at either end. The nearer one had the usual red letters: TIDES RISE QUICKLY. DO NOT CROSS OUTSIDE SAFE TIMES. Beneath it, screwed into a glass-fronted case, the harbour tide board listed yesterday's low water in black plastic numbers.

Low water: 21:40.

Rowan knew enough, without opening an app, to distrust it. She had grown up with the tide as a second clock. The evening spring ebb had been earlier than that. Much earlier.

"Where's the harbourmaster?"

Kit pointed to a woman standing beyond the ambulance crew, one hand on the rail, her face turned towards the island. Mara Fenwick had not changed as much as Rowan had expected. The same broad shoulders, the same dark hair cut at her jaw, the same habit of looking at weather as if it were an argument she intended to win.

Mara saw Rowan and did not smile.

"Bell," she said.

"Fenwick."

For a moment they were fifteen again on the harbour wall, both pretending not to be afraid of jumping. Then the moment shut.

"You knew him?" Rowan asked.

"Everyone knew Adrian. He made sure of it."

"That's not an answer."

Mara rubbed a thumb across the cuff of her oilskin. "Yes. He was on the heritage committee. Pain in the neck. Good on old maps. Bad with people."

The body lay face down, one arm crooked under him, the other stretched towards the island. Adrian Rusk had been a tall man, made awkward by death and water. His grey hair was plastered over one ear. A dark bruise showed at the left temple where the skin had split against bone or stone. His coat had ridden up, exposing the belt of his cord trousers. One brown shoe remained on his foot. The other was gone.

Rowan crouched at the edge of the scene and let herself look slowly. That was the first discipline: do not decide too soon.

There was weed snagged at his sleeve, as expected. Sand on the cuffs, as expected. A smear of dark grit on the back of one hand, not quite the same as the pale beach sand around him. A line of waxy residue on the collar of his coat, as if something polished had rubbed there. His right trouser pocket had been turned partly inside out.

"Paramedics?"

"Declared at six twenty-eight," Kit said. "No resuscitation attempted. He'd been in the water for hours."

"Any ID?"

"Wallet still in inside pocket. Cash untouched. Phone in waterproof pouch, dead from impact or water ingress. No notebook."

Rowan looked up. "Why mention a notebook?"

Mara answered before Kit could. "Because Adrian always had one. Little black thing, elastic round it. Wrote down everything you said, especially if you wished he wouldn't."

The gulls rose as a group from the fish market roof, white bodies flicking in the wind. Out on the island, Cormorant House showed its broken windows to the shore. The old quarantine building had been empty for most of Rowan's life. In childhood it had seemed romantic. Later she learned it was merely damp, unsafe, and expensive to save, which explained why Theo Sparke now wanted to wrap it in glass and sell it as heritage apartments to people who did not know what a winter tide could do.

"Who last saw Rusk alive?" Rowan asked.

"He was at the Lookout Arms about half seven," Mara said. "Arguing."

"With whom?"

"Depends who you ask. Theo Sparke, Nessa Quill, half the bar by the end. He had a talent."

"About the development?"

Mara's mouth tightened. "About the Mercy Gale."

The name landed between them like a dropped tool. Even Kit, who was not local, had heard of it by then. Every town had its old disaster, polished by retelling until it became less an event than a moral possession. Pelham Hard had the Mercy Gale: November 1998, lifeboat out in impossible weather, two men dead, a third disgraced, the Sparke family praised for raising money afterwards until their name was welded to courage.

Rowan's father had been on that boat. He had lived. He had said almost nothing about it in the twenty-eight years since.

"What was Rusk saying about it?" she asked.

"That everyone had got it wrong."

"Did he say how?"

"He said he had proof."

Rowan stood. The wind carried the smell of diesel from the harbour and something sweeter underneath, the rotten vegetable breath of the flats. The tide had drawn back now far enough to expose the lower stones. Water still moved through the gaps, quick and glittering.

"The tide board says low water was twenty-one forty," she said.

Mara looked at the sign, then away. "If it says that, it's wrong."

"How wrong?"

"Twenty-seven minutes. Give or take."

"Enough to strand a man who thought he had time."

"Adrian wasn't a tourist."

"No," Rowan said. "He was a historian with a missing notebook, a head injury, and an argument in the pub."

Mara's eyes shifted back to the body.

Kit said, "Accident until proven otherwise?"

Rowan watched one of the cormorants lift from the island roof and skim low over the causeway. It passed over Adrian Rusk without turning its head.

"No," she said. "The other way round."

# Chapter 2: The Tide Board

By nine o'clock, Pelham Hard had done what Pelham Hard did best. It had made itself small and busy.

The fishmonger opened late and blamed the police tape. The bakery put a tray of buns in the window as if sugar might steady the place. Outside the chandlery, three retired men in identical flat caps stood with their backs to the wind and claimed, in turn, that they had always known Adrian Rusk would come to trouble, that nobody could have foreseen such a thing, and that the council should have closed the causeway years ago.

Rowan took the harbour office before the rumours warmed through.

It was a square room above the stores, with a view across the quay and a smell of salt, printer ink, and old damp carpet. Tide tables were pinned to one wall. Keys hung in a locked cabinet behind the desk, each with a plastic tag written in Mara Fenwick's neat block capitals.

Mara opened the tide-board file without being asked. "Official printout from the harbour app. Yesterday's evening low: twenty-one thirteen. Safe crossing window should have ended by twenty-one thirty at the latest. On a spring tide, earlier if you're cautious."

Rowan looked at the paper. "The board on the beach said twenty-one forty."

"Yes."

"When did you set it?"

"Seven thirty yesterday morning."

"To twenty-one thirteen?"

"Yes."

"Who can change it?"

Mara took a breath through her nose. "Me. Assistant harbourmaster. Two quay wardens. Coastguard box has a spare. Lifeboat station has a spare. Museum has one for school tours, because God forbid a child should have to look through smeared glass. And the council office has a master key they think I don't know about."

"So half the town."

"The careful half."

Kit, standing by the window with his notebook, said, "Any CCTV on the board?"

"No. On the harbour mouth and fuel berth, yes. On a warning sign everyone ignores until they need someone to blame, no."

Rowan walked to the key cabinet. "Any keys missing?"

"Not now."

"That's not what I asked."

Mara's jaw moved. "The museum key was missing for three hours last week. Nessa Quill reported it herself. She found it in the archive sink, which tells you more about the state of that building than about criminal genius."

"And yesterday?"

"I didn't audit the keys yesterday."

"Why not?"

"Because I run a harbour, Rowan, not a prison."

The use of her first name was a little push. Rowan let it go. "Where were you between seven and ten last night?"

"Here until eight. Then home."

"Alone?"

"Yes."

"Can anyone confirm that?"

"My electricity meter, if it's chatty."

Kit did not look up, but Rowan felt him register the answer. Mara had always lied badly when cornered. Not because she lacked intelligence, but because contempt arrived before strategy.

Rowan turned back to the desk. Adrian Rusk's phone lay in an evidence bag beside his wallet. The phone had not died entirely. A technician had coaxed enough from it to recover the last few notifications, no content yet, only times and senders.

"Rusk received a text at eighteen fifty-two," Kit said. "Unknown number. Burner, likely. We have the first line from notification preview: 'Bring the page. Cormorants know the rest.'"

Mara frowned. "What page?"

"You tell us."

"I don't know."

"He was researching the Mercy Gale," Rowan said. "Had he found something?"

Mara folded her arms. "Adrian always found something. Mostly offence."

"You said he claimed he had proof."

"He did. At the pub. He waved a piece of paper around until Nessa told him to put it away before he got beer on it."

"What did it show?"

"I wasn't close enough."

"Mara."

"It looked like a log page," she said. "Harbour log, maybe. Old. Water-damaged."

Outside, a forklift beeped along the quay. A crate of sole went past the window, silver and flat as thrown knives.

Rowan said, "Why would a harbour log matter?"

Mara looked at the tide tables on the wall. "The night of the Mercy Gale, the harbour log went missing. Officially, it was ruined by flood water. People have been arguing about that since I was fourteen."

"And unofficially?"

"Unofficially, it said things people didn't want said."

Kit closed his notebook. "About Christopher Sparke?"

The room altered. Not visibly. No door opened, no floorboard shifted. But Mara's face became a harbour door in bad weather: barred from inside.

"You should talk to the Sparkes yourself," she said.

"We will."

"Theo will act like a fool. Don't mistake that for depth. Eleanor's the one who remembers everything."

Rowan looked again at the key cabinet. "Does Eleanor Sparke have a tide-board key?"

"Not officially."

"And unofficially?"

Mara gave a small, humourless laugh. "Eleanor has keys to rooms that haven't been built yet."

By ten thirty, Kit had the harbour camera footage. It showed Adrian Rusk at 20:18, walking alone past the fuel berth, away from the pub and towards the derelict sail lofts. He wore the same brown coat recovered from the causeway. He carried something under his arm, flat and wrapped in newspaper. Ten minutes later the camera caught the blur of a dark car on the service road behind the lofts. The plate was unreadable because rain had smeared the lens.

"Not the route to the island," Kit said.

"No," Rowan said. "It's the route to the old kiln beach."

"Which is?"

"Where you launch if you don't want the harbour camera seeing you launch."

Kit watched the footage again. "You said that like someone who once launched there for reasons her father never heard about."

"My father heard about everything. Usually before I got home."

The joke cost more than it should have. Max Bell was in his bungalow above the allotments, probably listening to Radio 4 too loudly and pretending not to wait for her call. Rowan had not told him about Adrian yet. She was not sure whether she was protecting him from shock or herself from the questions.

At noon the pathologist rang with the preliminary view. Drowning was likely, but the injury to Adrian's temple had occurred before death. A fall could explain it. So could a blow. There were fibres caught in the split skin: dark wool, perhaps from a glove. There was no sign of robbery beyond the missing notebook and whatever paper he had carried under his arm.

Rowan wrote it down.

Then she looked at the harbour tide printout again, at the false time behind glass, at the neat lie sitting where public safety should have been.

Some murders shouted. This one had adjusted a number and let the sea speak.

# Chapter 3: Archive Dust

Pelham Hard Museum had a smugglers' lantern in the front window and a handwritten sign apologising for irregular opening hours. Rowan had always thought both were honest advertising.

Inside, the ground floor was arranged for school parties and wet Tuesdays: model trawlers in glass cases, a stuffed gull with one furious yellow eye, sepia photographs of men in ganseys, and a display about the Mercy Gale set under a lifeboat-orange board. Christopher Sparke's portrait occupied the centre. He stood in evening dress at a fundraising dinner, one hand on a silver cup, handsome in the smooth way of men used to being thanked.

Nessa Quill met them at the foot of the narrow stairs.

"If this is about Adrian's papers, I already boxed what he left here," she said.

She was thirty at most, with cropped fair hair, ink on two fingers, and the pale indoor look of someone who spent her best hours with dead people's handwriting. Grief had not reached her cleanly. Her eyes were red, but her voice had sharpened itself against use.

"You were working with him," Rowan said.

"He was working near me. Adrian did not work with people. He harvested them."

"You argued in the pub."

"Everyone argued in the pub. Pelham Hard would lose half its economy without disagreement."

The archive occupied two rooms above the public displays. The first held map drawers and a table under a skylight. The second was no wider than a corridor, lined with shelves and archive boxes. The air tasted of paper, dust, and the faint mineral damp of old stone.

Nessa put a cardboard box on the table. "This was Adrian's current material. Photocopies, transcripts, notes on the Mercy Gale, planning objections, and one truly unhinged letter to the council about interpretive signage."

Kit lifted the top folder. "No black notebook?"

"No. He had it with him last night."

"And the page he waved around?"

Nessa's face changed too quickly. It became blank, which was an answer in itself.

Rowan pulled out a chair. "Sit down."

"I prefer standing."

"I prefer honesty, but we're all making compromises."

For a moment Nessa looked as though she might tell Rowan to get out. Then she sat.

"It was a harbour log page," she said. "Or part of one. November 1998. The ink was damaged, but there were call signs and times. Adrian thought it proved the Sparke launch came in before the lifeboat was damaged, not after."

Kit glanced at Rowan. "Why does that matter?"

Nessa pressed both palms flat on the table. "The official account says Christopher Sparke tried to help after the lifeboat was already in trouble. If his launch was in the channel before the collision, then he was not a rescuer. He was part of the incident."

Rowan let the phrase sit. Part of the incident. A museum phrase, careful and bloodless.

"Where did Adrian get the page?"

"He wouldn't say."

"But you know."

"I suspect."

"Say the suspicion."

Nessa looked towards the second room. "Lily Tye brought in a rusted biscuit tin two weeks ago. She's one of our volunteers. She mudlarks under the old sail lofts, which I have told her not to do because the wall is rotten and the council will blame me when it collapses. The tin had buttons, clay pipe stems, a brass tag from the old lifeboat shed, and scraps of paper stuck together with mud."

"Including the log page."

"I did not realise at first. Adrian did. He came in while I was trying to separate them. He became extremely still, which with Adrian was as close as he got to religious experience."

"Where's the tin now?"

"Locked in the conservation cupboard."

Nessa went to fetch it. Kit watched her cross the room. "She is either frightened or very angry."

"Both can be true."

The tin smelled of iron and creek mud. Inside, each object sat in a labelled tray. The brass tag read PHLB 3. One clay pipe stem. Two blackened buttons. A twist of green glass. A strip of paper under a transparent sleeve, its writing mostly dissolved.

Rowan leaned over it.

Only fragments remained legible:

21:02 OSPR...

... no light shown

LANYON aboard

... tow cut by C.S.

Kit read silently, then said, "C.S. could be Christopher Sparke."

"It could be Coast Station," Nessa said.

"You don't sound convinced."

"I'm paid to be precise, not comforting."

Rowan looked at the public display downstairs through the stairwell gap. Christopher Sparke smiled from his orange board.

"Who knew Lily found this?"

"Adrian. Me. Lily, obviously. I told the chair of trustees there might be a significant Mercy Gale item requiring conservation funding."

"Who is chair?"

Nessa's expression answered before she did. "Eleanor Sparke."

Kit exhaled softly.

At the far end of the archive, a floorboard creaked. Rowan turned.

A girl stood half in the doorway, rain-spotted parka zipped to the chin, phone gripped in one hand. Seventeen, maybe. Dark curls escaping from a wool hat. She looked at the tin on the table and went white.

"Lily?" Rowan said.

The girl backed away.

Nessa stood. "Lily, wait."

But Lily Tye had already turned. Her trainers hammered down the stairs, past the smugglers' lantern, out into the street. The front bell gave a frantic little jangle.

Kit moved towards the stairs.

Rowan stopped him. "No. Let her get as far as the corner."

"Why?"

"Because if she's running from us, we can find her. If she's running from someone else, I want to know who watches her go."

They reached the front window in time to see Lily cross the road towards the quay. On the opposite pavement, under the striped awning of the closed ice-cream shop, Theo Sparke stood with a takeaway coffee in one hand and his phone in the other.

He watched Lily run.

Then he looked up at the museum window and saw Rowan looking back.

Theo smiled as if caught doing something charming. It was a good smile, expensive and practised. It did not reach his eyes.

# Chapter 4: The Mercy Gale

Rowan postponed her father until late afternoon, which was both practical and cowardly. She told herself she needed the archive copies first. She told herself Kit could interview Theo Sparke without her for twenty minutes. She told herself many useful things while driving up the hill to the bungalow where Max Bell had lived since her mother died.

He opened the door before she knocked.

"Police car gives you away," he said.

"It's a pool car. It gives everyone away."

Max Bell had shrunk in the ordinary, infuriating manner of ageing men who had once seemed built into the world. His shoulders were narrower. His beard had gone white. But his eyes were still the exact blue Rowan remembered from childhood, a startling colour in a weathered face.

The sitting room smelled of tea, furniture polish, and the sea because all houses in Pelham Hard eventually did. On the mantelpiece stood three photographs: Rowan at graduation, her mother laughing at something outside the frame, and the lifeboat crew in 1998, taken six months before the Mercy Gale.

Max saw her looking.

"You're here about Adrian Rusk."

"You heard."

"I may be elderly, not buried."

"Dad."

"Mara rang."

Of course she had. Rowan took the armchair opposite him. The upholstery was worn where her mother's hands had rested for years. "Adrian was researching the Mercy Gale."

Max turned his mug by the handle. "Adrian researched whatever made people shut doors."

"Did he speak to you?"

"Several times. I told him what I told the inquest."

"Which was?"

"Bad night. Bad water. Worse luck."

"That's not evidence."

"It was enough for the inquest."

Rowan felt the old irritation rise, hot as fever. Her father could be affectionate, funny, generous, brave. He could also close a subject so completely that a person might bruise herself against it for years.

"There may be a harbour log page," she said. "It suggests Christopher Sparke's launch was involved before the lifeboat took damage."

Max closed his eyes.

The movement frightened her more than denial would have.

"Did you know?" she asked.

"I knew the sea was full of boats that night."

"Dad."

"No." He opened his eyes. "I don't know what you mean by know. People think memory is a rope. Pull one end and the whole thing comes in. It isn't. It comes up in weeded bits."

"Then give me the bits."

For a while he listened to the house settling around them. A gull screamed down by the allotments. The central heating ticked in the pipes.

"We got the shout at twenty past nine," he said. "Launch in distress near the outer channel. Weather already foul. Wind south-west, too much of it. We went out because that's what you do."

"Who was on the launch?"

"Christopher Sparke. Eleanor. One of their guests, I think. Maybe two. They'd been at some dinner along the coast and thought they could beat the weather home."

"Could they?"

Max gave her a look. "No."

"What happened?"

"We reached them off St Osyth's Eye. Their engine had failed. They were drifting wrong. We got a towline across, or Eddie did. Eddie Lanyon. Nineteen, keen as paint, hands quicker than thought."

He stopped.

Rowan waited.

"The line went," he said. "Officially Eddie cut it in panic after it fouled. That was what Christopher said. Eddie was washed over before anyone could ask him. Jack Prowse went after him. We lost both."

"And unofficially?"

Max's hands tightened around the mug until Rowan thought it might crack.

"I saw a light where there shouldn't have been a light."

"On the Sparke launch?"

"A torch, maybe. Low down by the stern. Then the line jerked. Then their boat slewed towards us and hit. After that it was noise."

"Did you tell the inquest?"

"I said there was confusion."

"That isn't the same."

"No."

The word sat there, plain and unforgivable.

Rowan looked at the crew photograph. Her father in the back row. Young. Broad. Beside him a boy with a grin too large for his face: Eddie Lanyon, scapegoat by obituary.

"Why didn't you say more?"

Max put the mug down carefully. "Because Christopher Sparke had three lawyers and a wife who could cry without her face moving. Because Eddie was dead and his mother had already buried two sons. Because the lifeboat needed money. Because I was a coward. Choose whichever helps your report."

It was the first honest answer and the cruelest. Rowan had wanted a villain and been handed a man.

"Adrian found proof," she said.

"Then he was in danger."

"From whom?"

Max's laugh was dry and brief. "You still think danger is a person with a knife. Sometimes it's a room full of respectable people who all need the same lie."

On her way out, he called her back.

"Ro."

She turned at the door.

"Eleanor came here last week."

Rowan went still. "Why?"

"To ask if Adrian had been troubling me."

"What did you say?"

"I told her he had come round with his notebook and his clever questions."

"Did you tell her what you remembered?"

Max looked past her, through the hall window, towards the sea he could no longer see from the chair. "I told her I was tired."

It might have been true. It might also have been the only lie left to him.

Back at the station room they had borrowed from the council, Kit had pinned photographs to a whiteboard: Adrian on the causeway, the tide board, Theo outside the museum, the harbour log scrap, the route from pub to sail lofts.

"Theo Sparke says he argued with Adrian about defamatory nonsense," Kit said. "Then he left the pub at eight, walked home, made three calls to investors, and did not murder anyone because murder is bad for planning optics."

"Did he phrase it like that?"

"Almost exactly. I admired the economy."

Rowan added Eleanor Sparke's name under Theo's and drew a line to the harbour log.

Kit watched her. "Your father?"

"He saw enough in 1998 to know the official account was wrong."

"Can we use him?"

The question was procedural. It still landed like a shove.

"If we need to," she said.

Outside, the evening tide began to turn. The harbour ropes tightened one by one, each boat answering the pull before any person noticed.

# Chapter 5: Black Sand

The old sail lofts crouched at the eastern end of the harbour, three long buildings with tarred boards, patched slate, and warning notices fixed to every door. In summer, visitors photographed them as picturesque decay. In winter, with rain coming sideways across the yard, they looked like what they were: rot with a view.

Theo Sparke had printed them differently. His planning boards showed warm brick, brass lamps, balconies, potted olives, and a woman in white linen holding coffee where generations of men had once cursed into their sleeves while mending canvas. SPARKE HARBOUR QUARTER, the largest board read. HISTORY, REIMAGINED.

Someone had written in black marker beneath it: HISTORY, EVICTED.

Kit studied the graffiti. "Concise."

"Pelham Hard has always had literary ambition."

The strip of beach behind the lofts was not like the shingle under the promenade. It was narrow, dark, and gritty, the remains of an old kiln and centuries of boat repair. The sand clung to soles in black crescents. It had clung to Adrian Rusk's cuff as well.

Rowan knelt near the slip. The tide had scrubbed most of the surface clean, but under the lee of a broken wall the grit still held marks: the double track of something wheeled, the crescent bite of a boat keel, and a partial boot print too smeared for size.

"Could launch a dinghy here," Kit said.

"People do. Quietly."

"Your tone implies personal history."

"My tone implies jurisdiction."

He smiled and took photographs.

The door to the nearest loft opened behind them. Theo Sparke stepped out wearing a waxed jacket too new to have earned its creases. He was fortyish, clean-shaven, good-looking in the manner of men who had been told so early and had never questioned the maintenance costs. His boots were muddy. His smile arrived before his welcome.

"Inspector Bell. Sergeant Shaw. I wondered when you would come to admire the future."

"We're more interested in last night," Rowan said.

"Aren't we all? Poor Adrian. Appalling business."

"You argued with him."

"Adrian argued at me. There is a difference."

"About the Mercy Gale."

Theo's smile thinned. "He had developed a theory. Retired men do. Some build model railways. Adrian accused dead philanthropists."

"Your father."

"My father, yes. Although dead philanthropist has a certain grandeur."

Kit said, "Where were you after you left the pub?"

"I gave you my calls."

"Calls can be made from many places."

"And murders can be imagined by policemen trying to look useful, but we must all resist temptation."

Rowan looked at the planning board. "Adrian's objection could delay your scheme."

"Everyone's objection can delay this scheme. That is the national talent. One man with a printer and a grudge can hold up forty jobs, twelve homes, six apprenticeships, and a sea wall Pelham Hard desperately needs."

"Luxury flats and a boutique hotel."

"With a sea wall."

"And Cormorant House."

Theo glanced towards the island. "Stabilised, restored, interpreted for public benefit."

"Sold."

"Maintained," he said. "Ruins are romantic until someone has to pay for scaffolding."

Before Rowan could answer, a dark blue Volvo turned into the yard. It stopped cleanly beside the planning boards. Eleanor Sparke got out with one gloved hand on the door frame and a silver-topped walking stick in the other.

She was smaller than Rowan expected. Age had refined rather than reduced her: white hair pinned low, navy coat, pearl earrings, a face composed around the assumption that others would wait until she finished speaking. Her stick touched the ground lightly. It did not seem necessary for balance. It seemed ceremonial, like a sceptre made acceptable by orthopaedics.

"Theo," she said. "You are keeping these officers in the rain."

"They chose it."

"Then we must admire their dedication." She turned to Rowan. "Inspector Bell. Your father was kind to me once. I have not forgotten it."

It was a neat opening, intimate enough to unsettle, public enough to deny purpose.

"I'll tell him," Rowan said.

Eleanor's gaze rested on her face. "Please do. How is Max?"

"Not part of this inquiry."

"Of course." A pause, almost a bow. "How may we help?"

"Did Adrian Rusk contact you last week?"

"Adrian contacted everyone. He had mistaken persistence for charm."

"About the harbour log?"

Theo looked sharply at his mother. Eleanor did not look at him.

"He claimed to have found a document," she said. "He also claimed my late husband was a coward, a criminal, and, if I recall correctly, a parasite in a blazer. Adrian favoured excess."

"Did you meet him?"

"I declined to."

"Did you text him yesterday?"

"I do not have his number."

Kit made a note.

Eleanor saw it. "That means you will now prove I did, which is fair. Please do."

Rowan looked at the stick. Its handle was shaped like a cormorant's head, silver worn smooth where fingers held it. A dark wool glove covered Eleanor's right hand. The wool was fine, almost black.

"Where were you between eight and ten last night?"

"At home. Alone until Theo came in shortly after ten."

"Can anyone confirm that?"

"My house has alarms, cameras, and a cleaner who believes dust is a moral failure. I imagine one of those may assist."

Theo shifted. It was small, but Rowan caught it.

"Problem?" she asked.

"No," he said.

"Then stand still."

For the first time, Eleanor Sparke smiled.

Back at the borrowed incident room, the pathologist's update waited in Rowan's inbox. The bruise on Adrian's temple was consistent with a rounded metal edge. Not a sharp fall against stone. A deliberate blow could not be ruled out. The fibres in the wound were dark wool, fine grade. There was a faint residue on the coat collar: beeswax and silver polish.

Kit read over her shoulder. "A polished metal object with wool nearby. That narrows it to every elderly person in Sussex in winter."

"Don't be ageist. It also includes half the middle-aged."

"You're thinking about Eleanor's stick."

"I'm thinking about evidence."

"Of course."

Rowan opened the scene photographs. Adrian's right pocket, turned out. Missing notebook. Missing log page. Head injury. False tide time. Black grit.

The killer had known three things: that Adrian had proof, that he could be lured with the promise of more, and that the tide would finish what a blow began.

Outside the council-room windows, gulls dipped and rose in the wind over Pelham Hard. Rowan watched them for a moment. Her father used to say gulls never wasted effort. They let the weather do the work.

So had Adrian's killer.

# Chapter 6: The Girl in the Boathouse

They found Lily Tye in the old lifeboat boathouse, which was no longer used for lifeboats and not quite used for anything else. It held stacked chairs for summer fetes, retired oars, three broken display boards, and a smell of dust over salt.

She had wedged herself behind a clinker-built dinghy with peeling blue paint and was eating crisps from a family bag with the grim concentration of the frightened.

"I'm not running," she said before Rowan spoke.

"You're hiding."

"Different."

"More honest, at least."

Lily glanced at Kit. "Is he nice?"

"No," Kit said.

She blinked.

"But I'm fair," he added.

That earned him the smallest possible smile.

Rowan sat on an upturned crate, leaving space between them. "Nessa says you found the tin under the sail lofts."

"I didn't steal anything. It was in the mud."

"I didn't say you stole it."

"Everyone says mudlarking is stealing when poor people do it and archaeology when people with degrees do it."

Kit looked down at his notebook, hiding amusement.

"Did Adrian know where you found it?" Rowan asked.

Lily picked at the crisp packet seam. "He asked. I didn't tell him at first. He got all excited, which was weird because it was mostly pipe bits and buttons. Then he said the paper mattered. Said it could clear a dead boy's name."

"Eddie Lanyon."

"Yeah. My mum knew his sister. Everyone did, apparently. This town is basically one big group chat with gravestones."

"Did Adrian take a page?"

Lily nodded. "Nessa said no, it needed preserving, but he said the tide wouldn't wait."

"What tide?"

"The cormorant tide." She looked embarrassed. "That's what he called it. The very low spring tide when you can get into the cellar at the island house. He said the birds knew because they moved down to the lower rocks. He made everything sound like a riddle even when he was asking for a stapler."

Rowan felt the investigation tilt. "He went to St Osyth's Eye before he died?"

"Earlier. Afternoon. He borrowed my head torch."

"Did he return it?"

"No."

"Did he say what he found?"

Lily shook her head, then stopped. "He said, 'There it is, the thing they couldn't drown.'"

"To you?"

"To himself. He did that."

Kit asked, "Why did you run from the museum?"

Lily's hand closed around the crisp packet until it crackled. "Because someone was in the archive last night."

Rowan waited.

"After Adrian died, I mean. I couldn't sleep, so I went to check the tin was still there. Stupid. The side door sticks if you know where to kick it. Someone was upstairs already. I heard boxes moving. Then I smelled this perfume."

"What kind?"

"Old-lady flowers. Sorry."

"Violets?" Rowan asked.

Lily looked at her. "Maybe. Like Parma Violets but expensive."

Eleanor Sparke had smelled faintly of violets in the rain.

"Did you see who it was?"

"No. I hid in the loo until they left."

"Did you tell Nessa?"

"She'd have killed me for breaking in."

"Lily."

"Fine. She'd have been disappointed, which is worse."

Kit said, "Was anything missing?"

"Adrian's photocopy folder was open. The Mercy Gale one. I think they took a photograph, maybe. I heard the phone click. Then I got scared and flushed the loo so they'd think someone was meant to be there."

"Good thinking," Rowan said.

Lily's face flickered, not quite ready to accept praise.

"Did anyone threaten you?"

She looked away.

"Lily."

From her parka pocket she took a folded sheet of paper and handed it over. It was cheap printer paper, damp at one corner. The words had been typed in a large plain font:

MUD KEEPS WHAT IT IS GIVEN. SO SHOULD YOU.

No signature.

"It was in my bike basket this morning," she said. "Mum thinks it's from some boy. I let her."

Rowan folded the paper into an evidence sleeve. "You're not going back to school today. Kit will take you and your mum to the station. We'll get a formal statement."

"Do I have to?"

"Yes."

"Will Nessa be angry?"

"Almost certainly."

Lily sighed. "Fine."

Outside, the boathouse doors banged in the wind. Rowan stepped into the yard first. Across the quay, Eleanor Sparke's Volvo moved slowly past the museum and up towards the High Street. It did not stop. It did not need to.

Kit came out with Lily a few paces behind him.

"Parma Violets but expensive," he said quietly.

"Put it on the board exactly like that."

"With quote marks?"

"With pride."

At the station, Lily's mother arrived in a supermarket fleece and a state of controlled terror. Nessa arrived ten minutes later and did, as predicted, become disappointed in a way that made Lily cry faster than anger would have done.

Rowan left them with Kit and returned to the archive with a warrant application already forming in her mind. The Mercy Gale folder was still open on Nessa's table. One document had been moved from its sleeve and replaced the wrong way round.

It was a copy of a 1998 invoice from Sparke Marine Services for repairs to a private launch named Osprey. The date was three days after the Mercy Gale. The listed work was bland: hull patch, stern rail, repainting. But the amount was not bland, and neither was the handwritten note at the bottom.

Urgent. No insurance. No report.

The initials beside it were E.S.

Rowan photographed the page, then stood in the quiet archive listening to the old building creak. The town had spent decades telling itself the sea had taken two men. But paper had survived in the mud, and paper, unlike people, did not learn to be grateful for silence.

# Chapter 7: Low Water

Low water came at 14:06, and with it the island revealed itself reluctantly.

The causeway emerged in patches: first the crown of the stones, then the weed-slick sides, then the channels between them where water hurried seaward in brown glass ribbons. Uniform kept the public back at the beach. A few residents gathered anyway, hoods up, pretending not to be watching a murder inquiry with the appetite of theatre.

Mara Fenwick stood beside Rowan at the warning board. "You've got forty minutes before I'd want anyone turning back."

"The table gives us fifty-five."

"The table wasn't born here."

Rowan looked at her. "You still say you were home after eight?"

"Yes."

"You know we'll check."

"I assumed policing had advanced that far."

"Mara."

The harbourmaster's face tightened. "I went out."

"Where?"

"To my father's."

"Why lie?"

"Because he was drunk, and because he told me he saw Adrian with a woman at the kiln beach, and because when I asked which woman he said, 'the one with death on her coat,' so I decided not to build your case on it."

"Your father is Patrick Fenwick."

"Yes."

"He was on shore during the Mercy Gale."

"Everyone was somewhere during the Mercy Gale. It's Pelham Hard's favourite alibi."

Rowan held her gaze a moment longer, then nodded towards the island. "You lead."

They crossed in single file: Mara first, Rowan behind her, Kit behind Rowan with a scene kit slung over one shoulder, and two search officers after him. The stones were treacherous underfoot. Weed slid and sucked beneath their boots. On either side, the exposed flats gleamed with worm casts and shallow pools. The air smelled metallic, stripped clean by the ebb.

At the island, Cormorant House rose from coarse grass and nettles, its brickwork furred with salt, its roof broken along one side. Birds shifted and muttered above the empty windows. The old boathouse leaned towards the channel as if considering surrender.

"Adrian came here in the afternoon," Rowan said. "He borrowed Lily's head torch."

"Then he was a bigger fool than I thought."

"You never came here?"

Mara gave her a look. "We all came here. It was where you went when you wanted to be older than you were."

Rowan remembered a bottle of cider, a dare, Mara's hand warm around her wrist as they ran back from the rising tide. Memory made children of them without permission.

The cellar entrance was half hidden by collapsed masonry on the seaward side. At ordinary low water it remained flooded. On a spring ebb, a narrow gap opened under the broken step, just high enough for a person willing to crawl.

Kit shone his torch inside. "Charming."

"After you," Rowan said.

"Rank has privileges."

Mara snorted and went first.

The cellar stank of brine, bird droppings, and old lime mortar. Water dripped steadily from the ceiling. Rowan's torch found rusted hooks, broken bottles, a crab moving with delicate outrage, and a recess in the wall where newer scratches marked the brick. Something had been pulled from there recently.

Kit photographed the recess. "The thing they couldn't drown?"

"Maybe."

On the floor beneath it lay a torn strip of newspaper, still damp. Rowan lifted it with tweezers. The date on the scrap was from the previous week. Adrian must have wrapped something here after finding it, or unwrapped something to carry away.

Mara, crouched by the steps, said, "Blood."

The stain was small, a brownish smear on the edge of a brick at shoulder height. Nearby, snagged on a nail, was a thread of dark wool.

"Not where he was found," Kit said.

"No."

Rowan looked back towards the causeway through the cellar opening. The killer had not struck Adrian on the exposed stones. He had been hit here or near here, where the old house kept wind and sound inside. Then moved, perhaps half conscious, perhaps already helpless, to the causeway. Left where the water would do the rest.

Something pale glinted in a crack near the wall. Rowan eased it free with the tweezers. It was a tiny crescent of mother-of-pearl, no larger than a fingernail clipping, backed by a smear of old adhesive.

Kit leaned in. "Button?"

"Inlay," Mara said.

Rowan looked at her.

"From a fancy stick or knife handle, maybe. My grandfather had a tobacco box with pieces like that."

Eleanor Sparke's silver cormorant stick had a mother-of-pearl eye.

Rowan bagged the fragment.

Outside, one of the search officers called from the grass. They had found Lily's head torch under a tangle of nettles, cracked at the lens. The battery still worked. On the elastic strap, half hidden in mud, someone had left a partial fingerprint in blood.

Kit's eyebrows lifted. "That would be helpful."

"Careful," Rowan said. "The case might hear you."

They searched until Mara's patience ran out before the tide did.

"Back," she said. "Now."

The return crossing was uglier. Water had begun nosing through the lower channels, filling spaces that had been stone ten minutes before. The causeway changed under their feet with each step. Halfway across, Rowan turned and looked back.

Cormorant House stood above the lifting water, windows black, birds hunched along the roofline. It was easy to see why Adrian had made a riddle of it. At the right tide, the island gave up secrets. At the wrong one, it kept them forever.

On the beach, a crowd waited beyond the cordon. Eleanor Sparke stood among them beneath a navy umbrella. When Rowan stepped off the causeway, Eleanor inclined her head.

Not greeting. Assessment.

Rowan held up the evidence bag just high enough for Eleanor to see the mother-of-pearl crescent.

For the first time since they had met, Eleanor Sparke forgot to arrange her face.

Only for a second.

It was enough.

# Chapter 8: The Net Loft

Silas Reed lived above the net loft behind the chandlery, in two rooms that smelled of tobacco, rope, and kippers. He had ignored three calls, one visit from a constable, and a note pushed through his door. At seven that evening his neighbour reported hearing a crash and "language unsuitable for any Christian wall."

Rowan found him sitting on the floor with blood down one side of his face and a broken chair beside him.

"Ambulance is coming," she said.

"Don't need one."

"Your head disagrees."

"My head's always been dramatic."

He was eighty-one, wiry, and furious at being seen vulnerable. Kit checked the rooms while Rowan pressed a towel to the cut above Silas's eyebrow. The little kitchen was tidy. The sitting room was not. Drawers had been opened, cushions thrown, framed photographs tipped face down on the carpet.

"Who did this?" Rowan asked.

"Didn't see."

"Try again."

"Door went. Thought it was you lot. Someone came up behind me. Next thing, floor."

"Man? Woman?"

"Heavy step. That's all."

"What were they looking for?"

Silas's eyes slid towards the cold fireplace.

Rowan followed the look. "Kit."

Kit crouched and felt along the soot-blackened bricks. A loose one shifted. Behind it was a cloth packet tied with string.

Silas swore with feeling.

Inside the packet lay three objects: a lifeboat crew photograph, a folded statement from 1998, and a small brass whistle greened by age.

"Adrian's missing whistle?" Kit asked.

Silas shook his head. "Eddie Lanyon's. Took it from the boat shed after they said what they said about him. His mother couldn't bear to ask for it. I meant to give it back and then it got too late, same as everything."

Rowan opened the folded statement. It was a draft, never signed. Silas Reed's name was typed at the top. The date was December 1998.

I saw Mr Christopher Sparke cut the towline between Osprey and Pelham Hard lifeboat. I saw Mrs Sparke standing beside him with a torch. Eddie Lanyon was forward at that time and could not have reached the stern cleat.

Rowan read it twice.

"Why didn't you sign?"

Silas stared at the opposite wall. "Because Christopher came to the quay with his lawyer. Said memories go funny in storms. Said if I made trouble, the insurance might not pay the lifeboat fund, and Eddie's mother would lose the hardship grant. Said people would ask why I was sober enough to remember but not brave enough to help."

"Were you?"

"Sober? No."

"Brave enough?"

His mouth worked. "No."

There it was again: not villainy alone, but a town made from small surrenders.

"Did Adrian know about this statement?"

"He guessed. Came badgering. I told him to leave dead boys alone."

"Did you give him anything?"

Silas nodded at the whistle. "He took that yesterday afternoon. Said if Eddie's name was in his talk, Eddie should have a voice in the room. Dramatic sod."

"The whistle wasn't on his body."

"Then whoever killed him took it."

Kit came back from the bedroom. "No forced entry. Back window open over the flat roof."

Silas snorted. "No one over fifty came through that."

"Theo Sparke?" Rowan asked.

"Maybe. He's got more hair oil than sense, but he's not soft."

"Eleanor?"

Silas gave her a look. "Eleanor never climbs through windows. She makes you open the door and feel grateful for the chance."

The ambulance crew arrived and began the gentle argument required to remove an unwilling old man from his own floor. Rowan stepped aside to take a call from forensics.

The blood on Lily's head torch was Adrian's. The partial fingerprint over it did not match Adrian, Lily, Rowan, Kit, Mara, Theo, or Nessa. Eleanor Sparke's elimination prints had not yet been provided. Her solicitor had asked whether an appointment next week would be convenient.

"Tell them no," Rowan said.

"Already did," the forensic officer replied.

At the hospital, Silas refused stitches until a nurse half his size told him to stop performing masculinity near her clean trolley. Rowan waited through the treatment and then took his formal statement in a curtained bay that smelled of disinfectant and vending-machine soup.

"There's more," Silas said at last.

Rowan lowered her pen.

"After the inquest, Eleanor came to see me. Not Christopher. Eleanor. She said Eddie's mother had suffered enough and didn't need my guilt dressed up as honesty. She said Pelham Hard needed a story it could live with."

"And did it?"

"Live with it?" Silas looked at his hands. "Look around."

On the drive back, Kit was quiet until the coast road dipped and the lights of Pelham Hard appeared below them.

"We have motive for Eleanor," he said. "Maybe for Theo if the development collapses. Opportunity depends on the tide-board key and the island. Physical evidence maybe points to her stick, but not enough yet."

"And someone assaulted Silas."

"Could be Theo cleaning up for his mother."

"Could be someone trying to make us think that."

Kit leaned his head back against the seat. "I miss burglaries. Burglars rarely have heritage committees."

Rowan almost smiled.

Her phone rang as they reached the harbour. The caller ID showed Max.

"Dad?"

For a moment she heard only his breathing and the faint murmur of the radio.

"I remembered something," he said.

"What?"

"The light on the Sparke boat. It wasn't a torch. It was Eleanor's cigarette case. Silver. Christopher used it to cut the line because the knife was in it."

Rowan pulled into the kerb.

"Dad, a cigarette case can't cut a towline."

"No. But it had the knife clipped inside. Fancy thing. Mother-of-pearl on the handle. She carried it everywhere in those days. Said a woman should be able to open her own parcels."

Mother-of-pearl.

Rowan looked across the harbour at Sparke House on the hill, its windows lit above the town like a ship that had never intended to answer distress.

# Chapter 9: The False Light

Eleanor Sparke received the warrant at half past eight in the morning wearing pearls, lipstick, and an expression of courteous injury.

Sparke House stood above the town behind flint walls and a garden clipped into obedience. From its terrace, Pelham Hard arranged itself beautifully below: harbour, church, sail lofts, causeway, island. It was the view printed on postcards and planning brochures, the view that made neglect look like potential.

"Inspector," Eleanor said, reading the warrant without haste. "You might have telephoned."

"Then it would have been a request."

"And this is theatre."

"This is a search."

Theo appeared behind her in a shirt buttoned wrong at the throat. "Mother?"

"Go and make coffee, darling. The police have mistaken decisiveness for evidence."

Rowan watched him obey. It was not fear exactly. It was training.

They searched the study first. It was a handsome room full of maritime paintings, leather chairs, and silver-framed photographs from charity dinners. Christopher Sparke looked out from several of them, sometimes in black tie, sometimes in sailing waterproofs, always lit by admiration.

Kit found the first useful item in the lower drawer of Eleanor's desk: a tide-board key on a brass ring, untagged, wrapped in a folded programme from a lifeboat memorial service.

"Not official," he said.

Eleanor, standing at the doorway with her solicitor on speakerphone, did not blink. "I have chaired public safety committees for thirty years. Keys accumulate."

"So do questions," Rowan said.

In the boot room they found a pair of navy rubber-soled boots with black grit in the tread. Eleanor said the grit came from inspecting the sail lofts with Theo. That was possible. On a hook beside the coats hung dark wool gloves. Eleanor said she owned many gloves. That was true.

In the hall stand was the silver-topped walking stick.

The cormorant head gleamed under the lights. One eye was mother-of-pearl. The other had been replaced with a bead of plain black glass, glued crudely into the socket.

Rowan did not touch it. "When was that repaired?"

"Recently," Eleanor said.

"By whom?"

"My hands are still steady enough for glue."

"Why not mention it when we found a mother-of-pearl fragment on the island?"

"Because I was not aware your fragment was applying for membership of my belongings."

Kit photographed the stick in place before bagging it. The solicitor's voice crackled from the phone, urging restraint in a tone that suggested both cost and exhaustion.

The alarm logs did more damage than the gloves. Sparke House had been unset at 20:04 on the night Adrian died and reset at 22:17. Eleanor said Theo must have done it. Theo said nothing until Rowan asked him in the kitchen, away from his mother.

"She was out," he said at last.

"Where?"

"I don't know."

"You told us she was home."

"I thought she had met Adrian. To pay him off, or frighten him, or do whatever people do when they have more nerve than judgment." He pressed both hands to his face. "I didn't think she had killed him."

"Why would she pay him off?"

Theo looked towards the study. "Because he had a page. Because if the Mercy Gale story fell apart, so did half the moral scaffolding this town has built around us. The development would be dead. The charitable trust would be investigated. Mother's reputation would be shredded."

"And yours?"

He laughed once, bitterly. "Mine is mostly laminate."

Rowan believed him more in that moment than she had when he smiled.

By noon, forensics had Eleanor's prints. By three, they had a match to the partial print on Lily's cracked head torch. Not complete, not pretty, but enough to place Eleanor's hand on the torch after Adrian's blood was on it.

At four, Kit came in with phone data.

"The burner that texted Adrian was purchased in Eastbourne eight days ago," he said. "Cash. No CCTV usable. It pinged off the Pelham mast twice on the murder night, then died. But one number called it that afternoon from a withheld landline."

"Sparke House?"

"No. Heritage Trust office."

Rowan closed her eyes for a second. Eleanor had keys to rooms that had not been built yet.

"Anything else?"

"Nessa found something. She says Adrian left a note in the archive margin. Not a note note. Adrian being Adrian."

The note was on a photocopy of an eighteenth-century island plan, written in Adrian's tight hand:

False light kept in bird house. Ask E.S. why she saved the knife.

Nessa stood beside the table, arms folded. "Bird house means Cormorant House. He was pleased with himself when he said it."

"False light?" Kit asked.

"In wrecking lore, false lights lured ships onto rocks," Nessa said. "Adrian used the phrase for any official lie. He had themes. Unfortunately."

Rowan looked at the island plan. A small outbuilding was marked beside the ruined boathouse, no longer standing.

"Could there be another hiding place?"

"There are voids everywhere," Nessa said. "The place is falling apart."

"If Eleanor killed Adrian for what he found, why leave anything there?"

"Because the tide was coming in," Kit said. "Because moving a body took longer than she expected. Because even murderers have bad time management."

Rowan thought of the false tide board, the altered number giving Adrian an illusion of time. Perhaps Eleanor had believed her own adjustment too. Perhaps she had not realised how little margin the island allowed.

They could apply for another search, flood the island with officers, and find everything or nothing. But if Eleanor believed Adrian had hidden proof in Cormorant House, and if she had seen the warrant, the missing eye, the key taken from her desk, she might do what frightened people did.

She might return to the one place she thought still contained her life.

Rowan looked at Kit.

"Low water tonight?" he asked.

"Twenty-three eighteen."

"I'll bring coffee."

"Bring Mara."

"You trust her?"

Rowan folded the photocopy and placed it in an evidence sleeve. "On a causeway at night, I trust the harbourmaster more than the table."

# Chapter 10: Cormorant Night

Night made St Osyth's Eye less picturesque and more honest.

The island was a black shape beyond the harbour lights, low against a sky without stars. The causeway showed in fragments under Rowan's torch, each wet stone slick as bone. Wind moved across the flats with nothing to slow it. Somewhere in the dark, cormorants shifted and made low, irritated sounds in their sleep.

Mara checked her watch. "We have thirty-five minutes on the island. No heroics."

"I dislike how often people say that to me."

"Then stop looking like you need it said."

Kit, behind them, said, "This friendship has texture."

"This friendship has evidence of previous offending," Mara said, and stepped onto the stones.

They crossed without torches for the first half, using the harbour glow and Mara's sense of the path. Two uniformed officers waited on the beach. Another pair watched the kiln slip from the sail lofts. If Eleanor came, Rowan wanted her seen. If she did not, Rowan wanted the island searched before weather took the chance.

They settled behind the broken wall of the old boathouse. Cold came up through Rowan's knees. Kit handed her coffee from a flask, which tasted of metal and poor choices. Mara stood listening.

At 22:54 a pale light moved on the water near the kiln beach.

Not a torch. Too low. A shaded lantern on a small boat.

Mara leaned close. "Tender. Electric motor."

The light went out. A minute later, wood nudged stone below the boathouse. Footsteps scraped on the slip.

Eleanor Sparke came into view wearing a dark coat and boots, one hand against the wall, the other holding a small torch with a red filter. No stick tonight. No pearls. Without her public arrangement, she looked older and more dangerous, not because age had given her force, but because it had taken away her interest in appearing kind.

She went directly to the landward side of the boathouse and knelt by a stack of fallen bricks.

Rowan waited until Eleanor had lifted the third brick and drawn out an oilskin packet.

"Mrs Sparke."

Eleanor froze. The torch beam held steady on the wall.

"Put the packet down," Rowan said.

For a moment, Rowan thought Eleanor might run. Instead, she stood very slowly and turned.

"Inspector Bell," she said. "You are persistent."

"It's in the job description."

Kit stepped out to Eleanor's right. Mara moved behind her, cutting off the slip.

Eleanor looked from one to the other. "You have made quite a production."

"Open the packet," Rowan said.

"I would rather wait for my solicitor."

"Then I will open it."

Eleanor held it out. Her gloved hand did not shake.

Inside was Adrian Rusk's black notebook, swollen by damp but legible, the missing harbour log page in a plastic sleeve, Eddie Lanyon's brass whistle, and a silver cigarette case. Rowan recognised the case before she opened it from Max's description: engraved initials, tarnished hinge, mother-of-pearl inlay chipped from one corner. Inside, clipped into a narrow slot, was a folding knife with a curved blade.

The knife had been cleaned. The groove near the hinge still held dark fibres.

Kit photographed everything.

Eleanor watched him. "You don't understand what that is."

"A knife used to cut a towline in 1998," Rowan said. "And evidence Adrian found before he died."

"You say used. You cannot know."

"Adrian knew."

The name touched something. Eleanor's mouth compressed.

"Adrian knew very little about mercy," she said.

The tide moved below them, a dark soft rush against stone. Mara looked towards the causeway.

"Five minutes," she said.

Eleanor smiled. "You see? The island dislikes conversation."

"Then we'll continue on the beach," Rowan said.

They started back with Eleanor between Rowan and Kit. The crossing had already changed. Water laced the lower stones. The gaps were louder. Halfway across, Eleanor stopped.

"Mrs Sparke," Kit said. "Keep moving."

She looked towards Pelham Hard. The harbour lights trembled on the water. For the first time that night, the polish left her voice.

"Do you know what that town would have done with the truth in 1998? Nothing useful. It would have devoured itself. Eddie was dead. Jack was dead. Christopher was destroyed in every way that mattered to me. What good would it have done?"

"Tell that to Eddie's mother," Rowan said.

Eleanor turned on her. "Do not presume to instruct me on grief."

The words cracked across the water.

Then her boot slipped.

Rowan caught her by the sleeve before she went sideways into the channel. Eleanor's weight pulled hard against her shoulder. Kit grabbed Rowan's belt. Mara swore, planted herself lower on the stones, and took Eleanor's other arm.

For three ugly seconds, all four of them were only bodies against water.

They got her upright. Eleanor's face was grey.

"Move," Mara said, and this time no one answered.

On the beach, uniform took Eleanor to a waiting car. She did not resist. She asked for her solicitor, her medication, and a blanket, in that order.

Rowan stood by the warning board, breath hurting in her chest, and watched the tide cover the first stones of the causeway.

Kit came beside her. "You all right?"

"Yes."

"That was an unconvincing pause."

"I'm all right."

He held up the evidence bag containing Adrian's notebook. "This may be our cleanest voice from beyond the grave."

"Adrian would enjoy that phrasing."

"I feared as much."

Mara joined them, wet to the knee and furious. "Next time you want to use my causeway as a courtroom, don't."

"Noted."

"No, not noted. Understood."

Rowan looked at her old friend in the harbour light. "Understood."

The tide moved over the false number on the beach board's lower edge, black and shining. By morning, the causeway would look innocent again. That was the trick of tides. They erased the scene without altering what had happened.

# Chapter 11: The Matriarch

Eleanor Sparke gave no comment for fifty-eight minutes.

She sat in Interview Room Two with a blanket around her shoulders, solicitor beside her, and a paper cup of tea cooling untouched near her hand. Without the house, the pearls, the view, and the correct chair, she seemed neither diminished nor exposed. She seemed concentrated.

Rowan placed each item on the table in its evidence bag.

The tide-board key. The glove fibres. The walking stick. The mother-of-pearl fragment. Lily's head torch bearing Adrian's blood and Eleanor's print. The notebook. The harbour log page. Eddie Lanyon's whistle. The cigarette case and knife.

Eleanor watched the procession as if judging table settings.

"For the recording," Rowan said, "I am showing Mrs Sparke item RS slash seventeen, a black notebook recovered from St Osyth's Eye on Thursday night."

"No comment," Eleanor said.

"Page thirty-two. Adrian Rusk wrote, 'E.S. wants private meeting. Says she has Christopher's diary. Bring log page. Cormorant House, after pub. Tide board says time enough, but check.'"

The solicitor leaned towards Eleanor. Eleanor did not move.

"He did check," Rowan said. "At least he tried. The harbour tide board had been altered. We recovered your key."

"No comment."

"He went first to the sail lofts, then by boat from the kiln beach. You met him at Cormorant House. He had Lily Tye's head torch. You brought the cigarette case because he had asked about the knife."

Eleanor looked at the bagged silver case then. Only briefly.

"He had already found it, hadn't he?" Rowan said. "In the old hiding place. Silas Reed hid the whistle and draft statement in town, but someone else hid the knife on the island. Christopher?"

At the name, Eleanor's expression shifted.

"Christopher was many things," she said.

Her solicitor touched her arm. "Eleanor."

She withdrew from the touch. "He was vain, foolish with money, and terrified of being ordinary. He was not evil."

Rowan said nothing.

Eleanor looked at the silver case. "The Osprey should never have been out that night. I said so before dinner. He laughed. Men like Christopher treated weather as something that happened to other people."

"What was on the launch?"

"Salvage." She said it with distaste, not guilt. "Coins, mostly. A dealer in Rye. Christopher had debts. He thought a little private enterprise would save everyone embarrassment."

"Then the engine failed."

"Yes."

"The lifeboat came."

Eleanor's eyes were not in the room now. "They were magnificent. That is the part people forget when they talk about lies. Those men came out in weather that made the deck vanish under them. Eddie Lanyon got the line across. He was smiling, I remember that. Smiling in that appalling rain."

For the first time, her voice faltered.

"Christopher saw the customs launch light beyond the harbour mouth. He panicked. If we were towed in, the cargo would be found. The debts, the salvage, the insurance, all of it. He cut the tow. He said he would reconnect it after we drifted clear."

"With your knife."

"It was in my case. He took it. I did not stop him."

"The Osprey hit the lifeboat."

"Yes."

"Eddie was blamed."

Eleanor's face hardened again, the old muscles returning. "Eddie was dead. Christopher was alive. Theo was twelve. The lifeboat fund needed money. Jack Prowse's widow needed money. Do you imagine truth pays school fees and mortgages? Do you imagine a town survives on purity?"

"Eddie's mother survived on a lie."

"Everyone survives on something."

Rowan let the silence lengthen. Eleanor had begun. People who began often hated stopping.

"Adrian found the log page," Rowan said. "He found the knife. He asked you to meet because he wanted you to confirm it."

"He wanted me to kneel," Eleanor said. "He wanted a performance of remorse he could quote."

"So you struck him."

"He said Christopher murdered those men. He said I had murdered Eddie a second time. He waved that wretched whistle at me." Her hand closed around nothing on the table. "I wanted him quiet."

"You hit him with the walking stick."

"Once."

"Then you moved him to the causeway."

Eleanor looked up. "He was breathing."

"Yes."

"I thought someone would find him before the water."

It was the first shabby lie she had told badly. Even her solicitor looked away.

Rowan said, "You altered the tide board before you met him. You created an accident and then used it."

Eleanor's mouth tightened.

"Why hide the notebook on the island?" Kit asked from the corner.

She seemed almost offended by the practicality of the question. "The tide came faster than I expected. Adrian was heavier than he looked. I had his things, the torch, the case, the whistle. I could not carry everything back and manage the boat. I meant to return before daylight."

"But the island was sealed."

"Yes."

"And when you saw us find the mother-of-pearl, you knew we were close."

Eleanor looked at Rowan. "You held it up like a school prize."

"It worked."

For a second, something like admiration passed across Eleanor's face, or perhaps contempt wearing the same coat.

"Do you know what your father said to me after the inquest?" she asked.

Rowan did not answer.

"He said, 'Let the dead rest.' Sensible man."

Rowan thought of Max in his chair, of guilt turning memory into weeded bits, of Eddie Lanyon smiling in the rain because he had not yet learned what the living would do to him.

"No," she said. "He was tired."

Eleanor looked down at the cooling tea.

The interview ended at 02:14. Eleanor Sparke was charged with the murder of Adrian Rusk before dawn, with further files opened on perverting the course of justice in relation to the Mercy Gale. Outside the station, morning spread thinly over Pelham Hard. The harbour looked washed and ordinary. Men unloaded fish. A delivery van reversed badly. The bakery lights went on.

The town had not yet understood that its favourite story had died in the night.

Rowan stood on the pavement with Kit, both of them too tired to speak for a while.

At last Kit said, "She almost made it sound reasonable."

"That was her talent."

"And yours?"

Rowan looked towards the harbour, where the tide board was being corrected under uniform supervision.

"Reading numbers."

# Chapter 12: After the Tide

Adrian Rusk's funeral took place on a wet Tuesday, which would have pleased nobody and suited him perfectly.

The church was fuller than Rowan expected. Not because Adrian had been loved. He had not made that easy. But he had been present in the town's life with such irritating force that his absence required attendance. Nessa Quill sat near the front, jaw set. Lily Tye sat beside her mother and cried with the frankness of someone young enough not to ration feeling. Mara stood at the back in harbour uniform. Theo Sparke came late and left early. No one stopped him.

Eleanor did not attend.

The vicar spoke carefully about truth, scholarship, and the courage to trouble settled waters. It was not a phrase Adrian would have tolerated, but the effort was decent. Outside, under umbrellas, people said the usual things in low voices. Shocking. Terrible. Who would have thought. Underneath, the harder sentences moved: I knew there was something wrong. My dad always said. Poor Eddie. Poor Jack. Poor everyone, once the lie had finished with them.

The council postponed the marina vote. Then, under pressure from the reopened Mercy Gale inquiry, the heritage trust withdrew its support. Theo Sparke issued a statement about reflection, consultation, and respect for community feeling. Kit read it aloud in the incident room with the flat brilliance of a man narrating hostage text.

Nessa began the work of rebuilding the museum display. She removed Christopher Sparke's central portrait herself. Lily helped carry the old board upstairs.

"We're not making a revenge display," Nessa told Rowan when she visited. "Just an accurate one."

"That may feel like revenge to some people."

"Good."

On the new temporary board, Eddie Lanyon's photograph stood beside Jack Prowse's and the other crew. Under it, in Nessa's precise lettering, was a single line:

The 1998 account is under formal review.

It was not justice. It was a door opened after too many years of being painted shut.

Rowan went to see Max on the Friday.

He was in the garden, pruning roses badly. Her mother had grown them with skill and a tolerance for thorns that Rowan had not inherited. Max cut one stem too low, swore, and looked up as if the bush had betrayed him.

"You'll kill that," Rowan said.

"Everything dies. Some things need encouragement."

She took the secateurs from him before horticulture became manslaughter.

Inside, she made tea. He had the local paper folded on the table. ELEANOR SPARKE CHARGED. MERCY GALE CASE REOPENED. Beneath it, a smaller headline announced storm damage to the east groyne, because life enjoyed scale more than people did.

"They'll want to speak to you again," Rowan said.

"I know."

"Proper statement this time."

"I know that too."

He sounded old. Not evasive, not defensive. Old.

Rowan sat opposite him. "You told Eleanor to let the dead rest."

He closed his eyes briefly. "I did."

"Why?"

"Because I was tired. Because I thought rest was all we had left to give them. Because I was wrong."

The answer did not heal anything. It did not need to. Rowan had solved enough cases to distrust sudden repair. People wanted confessions to clean rooms they had spent decades dirtying. Usually a confession only opened the window.

"Eddie's sister is coming down next week," she said. "Nessa found her."

Max nodded.

"You should speak to her."

"Will you come with me?"

Rowan looked at her father: brave enough once to go out in a storm, not brave enough afterwards to stand in a room. Both facts true. Both his.

"Yes," she said.

That evening, Rowan walked down to the harbour alone. The tide was low, the causeway open, the island dark against a washed orange sky. The corrected board showed the times in clean black numbers. A uniformed constable had been posted near it for the week, partly for safety and partly because symbols mattered when facts had been misused.

Mara was on the quay, checking mooring lines.

"You're off duty," she said.

"You're not."

"Harbour isn't fond of shifts."

They stood together without saying anything. Across the water, St Osyth's Eye held its ruined house and its roosting birds. The cormorants gathered along the roofline, ungainly and exact. One opened its wings to the last light.

"I should have told you about Dad sooner," Mara said.

"Yes."

"You could pretend to be polite."

"I've had a long week."

Mara accepted that. "He'll give a statement. Patrick. He says he saw Eleanor's boat coming back from the kiln beach. He thought if he kept out of it, no one would ask him about 1998."

"And now?"

"Now everyone is asking about 1998."

"Good."

Mara looked sideways at her. "Are you staying?"

The question meant in town, in the job, in reach of the past. Rowan watched water move through the harbour mouth, darkening as evening came on. For years she had thought leaving Pelham Hard made her honest about it. Distance had allowed her to dislike the place cleanly. Coming back had made everything less clean and more useful.

"For now," she said.

Mara nodded as if that were an answer the tide might respect.

At the warning board, Lily Tye was showing two tourists how to read the safe crossing times. She spoke with grave authority, pointing from the printed table to the water and back again. The tourists listened. People did, sometimes, when the person speaking had earned the right to be believed.

The cormorants lifted from the island one by one.

They flew low over the causeway, black against the fading sky, and for a moment their shadows passed over the stones where Adrian Rusk had died. Then they were gone towards open water, leaving the town with the tide, the truth, and the work of learning what to do with both.
